children: Travel disruption stretched into a third day Sunday as the effects of a more than four-hour groundstop continued to reverberate through airline operations.
Carriers have spent the weekend piecing themselves back together and rebuilding their schedules. But travel is still tough.

For travelers, it has been a slow and frustrating process. It has been one of the worst couple of days for travel this year, rivaling a severe winter storm that blasted huge swaths of the country in January.
More than 9,000 flights were canceled Friday. Saturday was only somewhat better: 6,600 flights were scrubbed. Another 1,300 were canceled as of Sunday morning.

Airlines worked to reaccommodate fliers over the weekend. American Airlines, for example, said it capped fares and added extra flights. But carriers still cautioned that recovery would take some time. Delta advised travelers with flexible plans to delay travel until Monday or later.

Airlines are accustomed to disruptions and go through a similar recovery process after blizzards, thunderstorms and their own technology snafus. But Friday's groundstop has little precedent in scope and duration.
"This is among the most significant operational impacts American has experienced," Heather Garboden, American's chief customer officer, wrote in a letter Saturday to those affected by the groundstop.

The Federal Aviation Administration's move to halt all flight departures came in response to problems within the outdated system that air-traffic controllers use to guide pilots through the nation's airspace.
FAA officials looking for the root of the issue zoomed in on a site in Arkansas, where a newly installed router began to ping the network at a very high rate, overloading the system.

The FAA doesn't know why the router went rogue. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the agency was zeroing in on a mechanical problem with the device itself or "incompetence" by L3Harris Technologies, which oversees the communications system known as FTI. An L3Harris spokeswoman said the company is supporting the agency's probe.
FTI is undergoing a multibillion-dollar upgrade. Duffy said that until all copper wires in the system are replaced with fiber at the end of 2028, more disruptions could come.

Friday's lengthy flight halt left thousands of planes and crew members out of place for their next flights. Some flights were scrubbed and never made it off the ground. Others turned back or diverted to alternative locations because overwhelmed airports didn't have space for them.
Pilots and flight attendants also hit limits on how long they can work and couldn't immediately be scheduled to work again. That set off a scramble for replacements.

Airlines offered additional pay for certain flights as an incentive for available pilots to pick up flights and raced to find hotel rooms. American allowed pilots and flight attendants commuting to work to book confirmed seats rather than chancing it on standby.
